paragraphs: This paper studies whether changing the importance of individual training examples can improve fairness while preserving predictive performance. Its intervention happens during training: examples receive different weights, changing how much they contribute to learning. The approach therefore addresses fairness through the training data rather than requiring a specialized classifier.

The central distinction is the level at which weights are chosen. Previous reweighing methods commonly give the same weight to every example within a group. Here, the authors estimate each example’s influence on both a fairness quantity and predictive utility. They then compute individual weights subject to constraints covering both objectives, allowing examples within the same group to contribute differently.

Experiments with standard classifiers and training procedures on multiple real-world tabular datasets support the approach. For equal opportunity, the authors report fairness improvements without an observed utility cost, whereas the compared methods sacrifice utility. This is an empirical result for the studied fairness objective and settings, showing that the usual tradeoff can sometimes be avoided.
icml-2022-achieving-fairness-at-no-utili.tldr: Weighting individual training examples by their influence improves equal opportunity without an observed predictive utility cost in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper develops a mathematical rule for improving a stochastic policy, which describes how an agent chooses among actions. The rule is independent of a particular parameterized function approximator. This makes the update a statement about policies themselves, rather than a procedure tied to one neural network or other chosen representation.

The authors derive the rule by solving a trust-region optimization problem in closed form using calculus of variations. A trust region controls how far a policy update moves from the current policy. Their derivation follows a new result that tightens existing policy-improvement bounds, and the resulting update carries a guarantee of monotonic improvement.

The rule also connects policy search with value-function methods. Because it does not require integration over states visited by the current policy, it can support the derivation of off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms. It further extends directly to cooperative multi-agent settings when agents update one at a time. That sequential-update condition is part of the stated extension.
icml-2022-an-analytical-update-rule-for-.tldr: A closed-form trust-region policy update guarantees monotonic improvement and supports off-policy learning and sequential updates in cooperative multi-agent systems.

paragraphs: BLIP addresses two problems in learning from images and text: models often specialize in either understanding or generation, and large web datasets contain noisy image-caption pairs. The paper proposes a pre-training framework that transfers to both kinds of tasks while improving the supervision obtained from web data.

Its central data-processing idea combines caption generation with filtering. A captioner produces synthetic descriptions, and a filter removes noisy captions. Together, these components bootstrap the text associated with images, making the training signal more useful. This gives the framework a way to improve how it uses available image-text pairs, alongside its ability to support different downstream tasks.

The authors report state-of-the-art results across image-text retrieval, image captioning, and visual question answering. The stated gains are 2.7% in average recall@1, 2.8% in CIDEr, and 1.6% in VQA score, respectively. BLIP also transfers directly to video-language tasks with strong zero-shot results. These findings support both the breadth of the framework and its ability to generalize beyond image-language tasks.
icml-2022-blip-bootstrapping-language-im.tldr: BLIP generates and filters captions to improve vision-language pre-training, achieving strong results across understanding, generation, and zero-shot video-language tasks.

paragraphs: MinHash produces compact random summaries for estimating Jaccard similarity in large binary datasets. This similarity measures resemblance between sets of present features. Classical MinHash theory relies on many independent random permutations, potentially hundreds or thousands per data vector, to obtain reliable estimates for tasks such as approximate neighbor search.

Circulant MinHash changes how those permutations are constructed and reused. It starts from only two independent random permutations and applies them in a circulant arrangement. The paper proves that this construction yields uniformly smaller variance in Jaccard estimates than classical MinHash using K independent permutations. Thus, reducing the number of independent permutations does not require accepting noisier estimates in the stated theoretical comparison.

Experiments support the proposed construction. The authors also introduce a simpler variant that uses just one permutation. Extensive numerical results show essentially the same estimation accuracy as the two-permutation version. The distinction matters: the two-permutation method has the stated variance theorem, while the one-permutation variant’s comparable accuracy is supported empirically.
icml-2022-c-minhash-improving-minwise-ha.tldr: C-MinHash uses two independent permutations in a circulant construction to provably reduce Jaccard estimation variance relative to classical MinHash.

paragraphs: Certifiable robust training uses mathematical output bounds to establish protection against bounded input perturbations. For deep explicit networks, these bounds can grow rapidly with depth, making training difficult. This paper investigates whether deep equilibrium models can offer a useful alternative, drawing on their effective infinite depth and controllable global Lipschitz behavior.

The main challenge is obtaining output bounds for an implicit model within a bound-propagation approach. The authors introduce an adjoint deep equilibrium model to approximate those bounds. They also apply weight orthogonalization and techniques tailored to equilibrium models to stabilize certified training. The resulting certifiably trained architecture is called CerDEQ.

On robustness tasks with an ℓ∞ perturbation budget of 8/255, CerDEQ achieves certified error rates of 64.72% on CIFAR-10 and 94.45% on Tiny ImageNet. The authors report state-of-the-art performance within the comparison class of models using regular convolution and linear layers. These results demonstrate a way to bring implicit equilibrium architectures into certified training despite the difficulty of computing their bounds.
icml-2022-cerdeq-certifiable-deep-equili.tldr: CerDEQ enables certified training of deep equilibrium models through adjoint-based bound approximation and training stabilization.

paragraphs: This paper models interactions involving several objects whose outcomes change over time. Tensor decomposition is commonly used for such interactions, but many methods discard timestamps, group them into discrete steps, or impose simple temporal models. These choices can make fine-grained dynamics and long-term interaction outcomes harder to capture.

THIS-ODE represents the evolving interaction outcome through a latent ordinary differential equation. A neural network learns how the hidden state changes with time. Representations of the participating objects determine the initial state and supply part of the network’s input. This links each object’s representation to the temporal behavior of the interactions in which it participates.

The authors also develop a learning procedure intended to make inference tractable and scalable. Forward sensitivity analysis computes gradients of the ODE state, and an integral transform supports stochastic mini-batch training. Results from simulations and four real-world applications demonstrate advantages for the approach. The contribution combines a richer continuous-time interaction model with machinery for fitting it efficiently.
icml-2022-decomposing-temporal-high-orde.tldr: THIS-ODE learns continuous-time dynamics of multi-object interactions using neural differential equations tied to object representations.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent learning, value decomposition helps assign credit to individual agents for a team’s outcomes. This credit guides agents that must act using their own information during execution. The paper examines the learning of this credit assignment through causal inference, focusing on a source of bias in existing decomposition methods.

The authors identify the environment as an unobserved common cause of both the global state and the joint value function. In their analysis, that shared cause creates a confounding path that biases credit assignment. Deconfounded value decomposition addresses this path using a trajectory graph constructed only from agents’ local trajectories. The graph serves as a proxy for the unobserved confounder.

DVD is designed to apply across different value-decomposition methods rather than being restricted to one architecture. Experiments on StarCraft II and MACO report consistent, significant performance improvements over several state-of-the-art decomposition methods. These findings support treating causal confounding as a practical issue in learning how individual agents contribute to collective success.
icml-2022-deconfounded-value-decompositi.tldr: DVD uses a graph of local trajectories to address causal confounding in multi-agent credit assignment, improving tested value-decomposition methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies how cooperating agents can receive useful individual learning signals when training is centralized but execution is decentralized. A team outcome alone does not explicitly allocate credit among agents. The authors focus on this allocation within multi-agent policy-gradient methods, where explicit credit assignment has received comparatively less attention.

They first analyze how reward shaping induces credit assignment and what bias it introduces into policy learning. This connects the usefulness of a modified learning signal with its potential to alter the policy update. Building on that analysis, they propose an exponentially weighted advantage estimator analogous to generalized advantage estimation. The estimator supports credit assignment while allowing a tradeoff with policy bias.

Empirical results show effective multi-agent credit assignment and substantial improvements over other advantage estimators. The contribution is therefore both analytical and algorithmic: it explains an interaction between credit and bias, then incorporates that interaction into an estimator. Its stated benefit is improved learning in the reported experiments while retaining a way to balance the competing effects.
icml-2022-difference-advantage-estimatio.tldr: An exponentially weighted advantage estimator improves multi-agent credit assignment while allowing a tradeoff with policy bias.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing certifies a classifier’s robustness by evaluating its behavior under randomly sampled input noise. Its certified radius can suffer from dimensionality-related limits. Double Sampling Randomized Smoothing adds information from a second noise distribution to tighten the robustness certificate for the existing smoothed classifier.

The added distribution supplies another sampled probability that constrains the certification problem. Under stated mild assumptions, the authors prove that DSRS can certify an ℓ2 radius scaling as Θ(√d), where d is input dimension. This result suggests that the framework may overcome the dimensionality barrier; the conclusion remains tied to the assumptions of the analysis.

The paper instantiates the framework for a generalized Gaussian smoothing family and develops a customized dual-optimization procedure that accounts for sampling error. This provides an efficient, sound way to compute the certificate from estimated probabilities. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet support the theory and consistently produce larger certified radii than the compared baselines across the studied settings.
icml-2022-double-sampling-randomized-smo.tldr: DSRS tightens randomized-smoothing robustness certificates using an additional noise distribution, with conditional theory and experiments supporting larger certified radii.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks propagate information across a graph, and those propagation rules strongly influence performance. Spectral analysis often describes a rule broadly as low-pass or high-pass. The paper argues that these labels do not explain why propagation rules with the same overall tendency can produce very different results.

The authors introduce concentration analysis to describe filters more precisely. It examines where a filter’s response is centered, how large its maximum response is, and the width of the response band. These three attributes expose differences that a broad low-pass or high-pass description can miss. The analysis also identifies limitations in existing propagation methods.

Guided by this framework, the authors propose Graph Gaussian Convolution Networks, or G²CN. Its propagation layer decouples the three attributes, giving the structure greater flexibility across graph types. Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art results on both homophily and heterophily datasets, where connected nodes tend to be similar or different, respectively. The findings support designing propagation around the detailed shape of its spectral response.
icml-2022-g-2-cn-graph-gaussian-convolut.tldr: G²CN separates three spectral filter properties to build more flexible graph propagation layers, achieving strong results across different graph types.

paragraphs: Training a graph convolutional network can become expensive because computing a node representation recursively requires information from neighboring nodes. Graph topology sampling reduces the graph information used during training, lowering memory and computation costs. Empirical studies have often found comparable test performance, motivating a theoretical explanation for when sampling preserves generalization.

This paper provides sufficient conditions on topology sampling under which training leads to diminishing generalization error. Its analysis covers networks with up to three layers for semi-supervised node classification. The conditions establish circumstances in which sampling works; they are not presented as requirements that every successful sampling method must satisfy.

The analysis also handles the nonconvex interaction between weights in different layers, an aspect less explored in earlier GCN theory. It explicitly describes how graph structure and sampling affect generalization and sample complexity. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. Together, these results help connect a practical scaling technique with guarantees about learning from limited labeled graph data.
icml-2022-generalization-guarantee-of-tr.tldr: The paper gives sufficient sampling conditions for diminishing generalization error in semi-supervised node classification with GCNs of up to three layers.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether an acceleration effect associated with Nesterov optimization can also improve sampling. The starting observation is that finite-step Nesterov updates can outperform their usual continuous-time limit. The authors seek sampling dynamics that retain the relevant extra structure and can produce accelerated gradient-based Markov chain Monte Carlo methods.

They rewrite Nesterov’s method for strongly convex objectives as a high-resolution ordinary differential equation that does not require a Hessian. A coefficient in this equation becomes a tunable hyperparameter. The authors then add appropriate noise and discretize the resulting diffusion process, turning the optimization-inspired dynamics into sampling algorithms.

For targets that are log-strongly-concave and smooth, the paper establishes acceleration over underdamped Langevin in W₂ distance, a measure of discrepancy between distributions. The result covers both continuous dynamics and discrete algorithms, and the acceleration is not merely an effect of rescaling time. Experiments show acceleration for log-strongly-concave and multimodal cases, with the latter extending the empirical evidence beyond the stated theoretical target class.
icml-2022-hessian-free-high-resolution-n.tldr: A Hessian-free, Nesterov-inspired diffusion yields sampling acceleration over underdamped Langevin for log-strongly-concave, smooth targets.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes stochastic gradient descent when the objective is nonconvex and gradient noise can have relatively heavy tails. Instead of describing performance only on average, it develops bounds that hold with high probability. It also studies optimization and generalization together, connecting progress on the training objective with performance beyond the training data.

The noise belongs to the sub-Weibull family, which includes sub-Gaussian and sub-Exponential distributions while allowing heavier tails. Under this setting, the authors establish best-known rates for general nonconvex learning. A gradient-dominance curvature condition gives faster rates, and an additional Bernstein-type noise condition sharpens the learning guarantees further.

The analysis shows how optimization and generalization tradeoffs depend on the conditions imposed. It also establishes that gradient clipping can remove bounded-gradient-type assumptions. In that clipped setting, the step size does not need knowledge of smoothness. The results broaden the noise behavior covered by high-probability SGD theory while making explicit which additional assumptions support stronger conclusions.
icml-2022-high-probability-guarantees-fo.tldr: The paper gives joint high-probability optimization and generalization guarantees for nonconvex SGD with sub-Weibull noise, with stronger rates under additional conditions.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph embeddings represent entities and relations mathematically so that a model can capture the graph’s relational structure. Their effectiveness depends on expressing both patterns among relations and the ways relations map entities to one another. The paper argues that existing approaches have insufficient capacity to capture these properties together.

HousE introduces a parameterization built from two types of Householder transformations. Householder rotations increase the capacity to model relation patterns, while Householder projections address complex relation mappings. These components serve complementary roles within a single embedding framework. HousE also generalizes existing rotation-based models by extending the rotations into higher-dimensional spaces.

The theoretical analysis establishes that HousE can simultaneously represent crucial relation patterns and mapping properties. Experiments report new state-of-the-art performance on five benchmark datasets. The combined findings connect representational capacity with observed benchmark performance: the framework supplies a mathematical way to express multiple aspects of relations together, and the evaluations show practical benefits in the tested knowledge graphs.
icml-2022-house-knowledge-graph-embeddin.tldr: HousE combines Householder rotations and projections to model knowledge-graph relation patterns and mappings simultaneously.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning trains representations using multiple views of a graph. Random changes can remove meaningful information, while manually preserving features using domain knowledge can restrict transfer to other domains. This paper proposes learning which parts of a graph should survive augmentation because they help distinguish that graph from others.

Rationale-aware Graph Contrastive Learning, or RGCL, uses a rationale generator without supervision signals to identify these salient features. It then creates graph views informed by the discovered rationales. The underlying idea is that useful augmentations should preserve the semantics relevant to instance discrimination. Pre-training on such views is intended to produce representations that support later fine-tuning.

Visual inspections on MNIST-Superpixel and MUTAG show that the generator identifies distinguishing semantic nodes. On biochemical molecule and social network benchmarks, RGCL achieves state-of-the-art performance. These findings provide two kinds of support: inspection connects the learned rationales to salient graph content, while downstream results support the effectiveness of using those rationales to construct contrastive views.
icml-2022-let-invariant-rationale-discov.tldr: RGCL learns salient graph features without supervision and uses them to construct contrastive views that preserve distinguishing information.

paragraphs: MetAug addresses how contrastive learning can obtain informative positive and negative features. Randomly augmenting input data does not always add useful information, which can limit the representations learned from the resulting views. The paper proposes augmenting features directly in latent space to learn discriminative representations without requiring a large amount of input data.

A meta-learning procedure trains the feature-augmentation generator by considering the encoder’s performance. This makes the generator responsive to how well its augmentations support representation learning. However, limited input data can cause the encoder to collapse to uninformative features, which also undermines the generator. The method adds a margin-based regularizer to discourage this degenerate mapping.

MetAug also introduces a unified contrastive loss designed to contrast all features within one gradient back-propagation step. The generator, regularizer, and loss address different parts of the same learning process: creating informative features, keeping representations useful, and training with those features together. Experiments report state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets.
icml-2022-metaug-contrastive-learning-vi.tldr: MetAug learns feature-space augmentations through meta-learning and combines them with anti-collapse regularization and a unified contrastive loss.

paragraphs: A density model needs both a way to generate samples and a normalization factor that makes its total probability equal one. These tasks can become difficult as the modeled function becomes more complex. This paper develops a neural representation that makes normalization and sampling efficient while retaining substantial expressive capacity.

For one-dimensional conditional densities, the network represents a cumulative distribution function. A generalized fundamental theorem of calculus then makes the normalization factor exactly and efficiently computable. The authors also derive a fast inverse-transform sampling algorithm, which generates samples by working backward through the cumulative distribution representation.

Extending these ideas to higher dimensions produces the Neural Inverse Transform Sampler, or NITS, for multidimensional densities with compact support. The framework is differentiable end to end and offers fast sampling alongside exact, inexpensive likelihood evaluation. On CIFAR-10 generative modeling and UCI density-estimation tasks, the reported results rival or exceed the state of the art, demonstrating applicability to realistic high-dimensional data.
icml-2022-neural-inverse-transform-sampl.tldr: NITS uses cumulative-distribution representations to combine efficient sampling with exact likelihood evaluation for multidimensional, compactly supported densities.

paragraphs: Gradient descent ascent alternates opposing objectives: one variable minimizes a function while another maximizes it. Earlier theory for a strongly concave maximizing variable required a step-size ratio scaling quadratically with its condition number. This makes the minimizing player move relatively slowly, whereas practical GAN methods often use similar step sizes.

The paper examines local convergence for general nonconvex-nonconcave minimax problems. It shows that a ratio scaling linearly with the maximizing variable’s local condition number is necessary and sufficient for local convergence to a Stackelberg equilibrium. The local scope is central: the result concerns convergence near the relevant equilibrium, rather than a guarantee from arbitrary starting points.

The authors also prove a nearly tight convergence rate and provide a matching lower bound. They extend convergence guarantees to stochastic gradient descent ascent and extra-gradient methods, then use numerical experiments to support the theory. The analysis narrows the theoretical step-size gap while precisely characterizing the remaining dependence on local conditioning.
icml-2022-on-convergence-of-gradient-des.tldr: A tight local analysis shows that GDA requires a step-size ratio scaling linearly with local conditioning to converge to a Stackelberg equilibrium.

paragraphs: The knowledge gradient algorithm is used to identify the best option among alternatives whose rewards must be learned through sampling. Although it is widely used, its complicated calculations make theoretical analysis difficult. Earlier results mostly described what happens as sampling continues indefinitely, leaving its behavior after a finite amount of sampling less understood.

Under independent, normally distributed rewards, this paper derives both upper and lower bounds on error probability and simple regret. These quantities capture the chance of selecting the wrong option and the loss associated with the final selection. Bounding them from both directions characterizes finite-time performance more fully than an eventual-convergence statement alone.

The resulting bounds also recover existing asymptotic findings as direct consequences. The authors examine knowledge gradient performance for the multi-armed bandit problem and describe how the analytical developments can support other improvement-based algorithms. Numerical experiments further illustrate finite-time behavior. The contribution makes the theory more relevant to decisions made with a limited sampling budget.
icml-2022-on-the-finite-time-performance.tldr: The paper bounds knowledge gradient’s finite-time error and simple regret under independent Gaussian rewards, extending its largely asymptotic theory.

paragraphs: Tensor networks represent large tensors using interconnected smaller core tensors. Choosing a suitable structure matters for compact representations. This paper focuses on a particular structural choice: how tensor modes are assigned to network vertices. It calls this problem tensor network permutation search and studies how to find useful assignments efficiently.

The theoretical analysis establishes counting and metric properties of the permutation search spaces. It also examines how the tensor network’s structure changes these properties. Using that foundation, the authors define neighborhoods for search and propose a meta-heuristic that samples randomly within a neighborhood, then repeatedly updates the neighborhood until convergence.

Across extensive numerical benchmarks, the algorithm reduces the model size needed for tensor network representations. The authors interpret this as evidence of improved expressive power through better assignments of modes to cores. The method also requires significantly less computation than the prior search method compared in the paper. The contribution connects search-space theory to a practical procedure for finding more compact tensor networks.
icml-2022-permutation-search-of-tensor-n.tldr: A theoretically grounded local-sampling search finds tensor-mode assignments that reduce tensor network model size in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Sparse-reward goal-conditioned learning gives an agent little feedback until it achieves its target. PAIR addresses this difficulty by alternating interaction-based reinforcement learning with supervised learning from successful experience. The approach separates collecting and improving behavior online from consolidating successful behavior using an existing dataset.

During the online phase, the agent trains with reinforcement learning and collects trajectories. During the offline phase, it learns from successful trajectories through supervised learning. The online phase also uses task reduction to generate more feasible trajectories and an intrinsic reward based on value differences to provide additional guidance when external success rewards are sparse.

The framework works with various online and offline reinforcement learning methods. On sparse-reward robotic control tasks, it substantially outperforms the reported non-phasic reinforcement learning and phasic supervised-learning baselines. The authors also report the first reinforcement learning method to learn six-cube stacking from scratch using only binary success rewards. This result illustrates how alternating exploration and self-imitation can support a demanding sequential control task.
icml-2022-phasic-self-imitative-reductio.tldr: PAIR alternates online reinforcement learning with supervised imitation of successful trajectories, enabling six-cube stacking from scratch with binary success rewards.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification asks a model to learn classes from very few labeled examples, typically one to five per class. Meta-learning prepares a model for this situation by training across other classification tasks. PLATINUM extends that strategy by using unlabeled data during meta-training to obtain a richer learned parameterization.

The framework uses submodular mutual information functions in both the inner and outer learning loops. These loops cover adaptation within a task and learning across tasks. Incorporating unlabeled examples at both levels allows them to influence more than the final classifier fitted to a small labeled set.

The evaluation considers unlabeled data drawn from the labeled classes and a harder setting that also includes classes outside that set. Experiments on miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and CIFAR-FS show improvements over MAML and semi-supervised approaches such as pseudo-labeling. The advantage is especially pronounced when labeled examples are scarce relative to unlabeled ones, supporting the framework’s use of abundant unlabeled data in few-shot learning.
icml-2022-platinum-semi-supervised-model.tldr: PLATINUM uses submodular mutual information to incorporate unlabeled data into both meta-learning loops, improving few-shot classification in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents need coordinated behavior, but strong statistical dependence between their behaviors does not by itself establish good teamwork. The paper shows that suboptimal collaboration can also have high mutual information. Consequently, maximizing mutual information without distinguishing the quality of the behavior can hinder progress toward better collaboration.

Progressive Mutual Information Collaboration, or PMIC, uses a criterion based on mutual information between global states and joint actions. It separates the learning objective into two complementary directions: increasing mutual information associated with superior collaboration and decreasing it for inferior collaboration. The first encourages useful coordination, while the second discourages becoming committed to poor coordinated behavior.

Experiments across a wide range of multi-agent reinforcement learning benchmarks report better performance than the compared algorithms. The results support a more selective use of dependence as a learning signal. PMIC’s contribution is to connect mutual-information optimization to the quality of collaboration, making the direction of the objective depend on whether the associated behavior is desirable.
icml-2022-pmic-improving-multi-agent-rei.tldr: PMIC encourages mutual information linked to superior collaboration and suppresses it for inferior collaboration, improving tested multi-agent learning performance.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimization adjusts gradient updates using information about the learning process. Under differential privacy, added noise can weaken the adaptive preconditioner that shapes those updates, reducing the benefit of adaptivity. This paper introduces AdaDPS to preserve that benefit by drawing the preconditioning information from a non-sensitive source.

AdaDPS uses non-sensitive side information to precondition gradients in private training. This changes how the adaptive component is obtained while keeping the optimization focused on the private learning task. The authors formally show that the framework reduces the noise needed for similar privacy guarantees, which improves optimization performance.

The empirical study uses simple, readily available side information and compares AdaDPS with strong baselines in centralized and federated settings. Across large-scale text and image benchmarks, the authors report an average absolute accuracy improvement of 7.7%, along with state-of-the-art privacy-utility tradeoffs. The findings support using appropriate non-sensitive information to improve adaptive private optimization without relying on noisy private information for every part of the update.
icml-2022-private-adaptive-optimization-.tldr: AdaDPS uses non-sensitive side information for adaptive gradient preconditioning, reducing required privacy noise and improving accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies how quickly accelerated gradient descent can reach an approximately stationary point of a nonconvex objective. Such a point has a sufficiently small gradient, so the target is a first-order stationarity guarantee. The analysis assumes both Lipschitz gradients and Lipschitz Hessians, controlling how rapidly derivatives change.

The proposed algorithm combines Nesterov’s classical accelerated gradient descent with a restart mechanism. It reaches an ε-approximate first-order stationary point using O(ε^−7/4) gradient computations. The bound contains no hidden polylogarithmic factors, improving the stated previous complexity by a factor of O(log(1/ε)). This makes the dependence on the requested accuracy sharper.

The method does not require explicit negative-curvature exploitation or optimization of regularized surrogate objectives. The proof is also simplified: it avoids relying on the analysis of strongly convex accelerated gradient descent, which the authors identify as crucial for removing the logarithmic factor. The contribution couples a simpler algorithmic structure with a tighter computation bound under the stated smoothness assumptions.
icml-2022-restarted-nonconvex-accelerate.tldr: Under Lipschitz gradient and Hessian assumptions, restarted accelerated gradient descent reaches approximate first-order stationarity in O(ε^−7/4) gradient computations without hidden logarithmic factors.
